solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Critic opinion of the unenlightened?

parts.note: a disapproving outlook, read playfully as the outlook held by dull, unenlightened people

explanation.surface: A reviewer sneers at the views of the ignorant masses.
explanation.walkthrough: To take this view of something is to disapprove; the question mark invites reading 'dim' literally, as the unenlightened whose view it is.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for a critical, disapproving opinion is also, read literally, the outlook of dim people.

clue.text: Comic hero's endless night in Hamlet?

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step

parts.note: Hamlet is the Prince of Denmark, a Dane

indicators.note: the final letter of the word for night is cut off, as if it has no end

parts.note: dark is the night, as in 'after dark'

explanation.surface: A cartoon hero's sleepless night spent in a small village, or at a Shakespeare play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamlet' looks like a small village but is the Danish prince; 'endless' drops the final letter of the night word before it goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The pilot of the future was the star strip of the British boys' comic Eagle, a classic comic-book hero.

clue.text: Fabulous sight, mind: a French star at twelve!

indicators.note: fabulous suggests something fabricated or fanciful, so the letters are made up anew

parts.note: un is the French for a

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a wondrous spectacle of a star shining at noon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fabulous' rearranges SIGHT MIND into MIDNIGHTS, then UN follows. 'Twelve' suggests noon, but the star is seen at twelve at night in polar summers.
explanation.definitionFit: In polar summer the Sun stays above the horizon all night, so that star is visible at twelve o'clock at night.

clue.text: Dearer pair relinquished? More reserved

indicators.note: relinquished says the couple of letters are given up and removed from the longer word

parts.note: dearer means more expensive, pricier

explanation.surface: Someone gives up a more cherished partner and becomes more withdrawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dearer' reads as more beloved but means more costly; 'relinquished' drops PR from PRICIER.
explanation.definitionFit: Cold in manner means reserved, so a frostier, more distant person is more reserved.

clue.text: Other half of footballer's story recounted in flyer

parts.note: a WAG is a wife or girlfriend of a footballer, his other half

indicators.note: a story recounted is told out loud, so the word is spoken and heard

parts.note: a story is a tale

explanation.surface: A tabloid tale about a footballer's partner, told on a flight.
explanation.walkthrough: WAG is British tabloid slang for the wives and girlfriends of footballers; 'recounted' gives TAIL from the sound of TALE.
explanation.definitionFit: A wagtail is a small bird, and any bird is a flyer.

clue.text: Tricky things to play in piano classes

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
ranks are classes or grades

explanation.surface: Difficult pieces to perform in piano lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tricky things to play' suggests hard music; these things are tricks that one plays on people.
explanation.definitionFit: Practical jokes are tricks, and one plays them on victims.

clue.text: Paid and trained: at any time killings his speciality?

parts.note: a pro is paid, unlike an amateur
trained means fit, in condition
e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, at any time

explanation.surface: A paid, trained hitman whose specialty is murder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Killings' suggests a hired assassin, but a killing is also a big financial profit.
explanation.definitionFit: One who makes excessive gains in hard times specialises in financial killings, that is, huge profits.

clue.text: Get a load of that missing heroin in old vessel

indicators.note: missing says the drug's letter is absent from the exclamation

parts.note: hark is an old command to listen, like 'get a load of that'
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that a cargo of heroin is missing from an old ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get a load of that' sounds like cargo but is an exclamation; 'missing' removes H from HARK.
explanation.definitionFit: Noah's boat that carried the animals through the Flood is a very old vessel.

clue.text: Central theme in books grasped by reformist, mostly

indicators.note: grasped by says the books are held inside the shortened name
mostly means the last letter of the name is lost

parts.note: John Maynard Keynes was the economist who reformed economic thinking
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: A main theme found in books held by a mostly reformist thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reformist' is the economist Keynes; 'mostly' trims him to KEYNE, which has 'grasped by' OT inside.
explanation.definitionFit: In music and speeches the principal idea or tone that sets everything else is its central theme.

clue.text: Fellow evidently about to drop off vital pump

parts.note: a person nodding is plainly about to fall asleep
a don is a university fellow
key means vital, essential

explanation.surface: A dozy man about to drop his vital pump.
explanation.walkthrough: The charade reads NODDING DON, a fellow evidently nodding off, then KEY.
explanation.definitionFit: An oil-well pumpjack bobs its head like a nodding animal, giving the pump its nickname.

clue.text: New Zealand port, one bringing in logs

definitions.meaning: a city and port in Hawke's Bay on New Zealand's North Island
John ..., the Scottish mathematician who introduced logarithms

explanation.surface: A New Zealand harbour where timber is imported.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Logs' suggests timber at a port, but these are logarithms, introduced by the Scottish mathematician.
explanation.definitionFit: The same name belongs to a North Island port city and to the inventor of logarithms.

clue.text: Misleading info put forward by a scoundrel

parts.note: a git is a contemptible person, a scoundrel
a prop is a forward in rugby, in the front row

explanation.surface: False information spread by a rogue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put forward' looks like a phrase for proposing, but 'forward' is a rugby front-row position, placed after the scoundrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Political propaganda, especially Soviet-style, is information meant to mislead.

clue.text: Instruction from ref: angry speech that can be ambiguous

definitions.note: a noun phrase: something that can be read two ways

parts.note: a referee calls 'play on' to let the game continue
to have words is to argue angrily

explanation.surface: A referee's instruction followed by an angry outburst that could be taken two ways.
explanation.walkthrough: A referee says 'play on' to wave play onward; 'words' as in 'having words', an angry exchange.
explanation.definitionFit: A pun deliberately exploits a double meaning, so it is language that can be ambiguous.

clue.text: Pants shed, liable to be in this state?

definitions.text: Pants shed, liable to be in this state?

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so the letters are rubbish and need sorting

explanation.surface: Someone whose trousers are off is likely to be in a particular state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' is the anagram signal on SHED LIABLE, and also the trousers removed in the surface; in British slang 'pants' means rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived word for being partly or carelessly dressed fits someone who has shed their pants.

clue.text: Stop publication on the web, attracting stick?

definitions.note: an adjective phrase used as a noun: a rod that attracts

parts.note: to bar is to stop
a mag is a magazine, a publication
the net is the web

explanation.surface: A demand to stop an online publication that is getting criticism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attracting stick' reads as drawing criticism, British 'stick', but means a rod that draws iron.
explanation.definitionFit: A straight rod that is magnetised is literally a stick that attracts iron.

clue.text: Sandy area close to pool one loved previously?

indicators.note: close to means the end letter of pool

parts.note: an ex is a former lover

explanation.surface: A sandy spot by a pool where an old flame was once met.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandy' looks like describing a beach area but is a name.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandy is a familiar short form of Alexander, as is this other diminutive.

clue.text: Led by boss, regularly put out flags

indicators.note: every other letter is put out, leaving the even-placed letters of these three words

explanation.surface: Under the boss's lead, flags are routinely put out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly put out' sounds like displaying flags but removes L, D, Y, O and S from LEDBYBOSS.
explanation.definitionFit: To flag is to weaken or decline, as the tide does when it goes out.

clue.text: One buzzing around organised quiz game

indicators.note: around says the buzzing insect goes round the other letters

parts.note: a bee is an insect that buzzes

indicators.note: organised means the letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A quiz contestant hits the buzzer at an organised quiz game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One buzzing' suggests a contestant hitting a buzzer, but it is the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a card game for two played with a double pack, popular in the nineteenth century.

clue.text: Run round in Ireland collecting fresh stock

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run

indicators.note: collecting says Ireland holds the other letters inside

parts.note: Eire is the Irish name for Ireland
pert means fresh, cheeky
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A trip round Ireland picking up new stock.
explanation.walkthrough: Eire is the Irish-language name for Ireland; the inserted letters go after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer's stock of pieces they are ready to play is their range of works.

clue.text: Briefing is formal, stylish and grand

parts.note: prim means formal and proper
in means fashionable, stylish
G is the abbreviation for grand, a thousand

explanation.surface: A briefing described as formal, stylish and impressive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand' is slang for a thousand pounds, abbreviated G.
explanation.definitionFit: Preparing someone with information beforehand is briefing them.

clue.text: ME airline, a casualty of America, turning bitter?

indicators.note: turning means the letters are read backwards up the down entry

parts.note: El Al is the Israeli airline, Middle Eastern
ER is the American emergency room, casualty in Britain

explanation.surface: A Middle Eastern airline becomes a casualty in America and turns sour.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the hospital emergency department is called casualty. 'Turning' reverses ELALAER.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitter is a British beer, and traditional cask beer of that kind is known by this name.

clue.text: To an extent, satirizing aristocratic amateur cricket club

indicators.note: To an extent says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Mocking, partly, an upper-class amateur cricket club.
explanation.definitionFit: This English wandering cricket club, founded in 1845, is famous for its aristocratic amateur members.

clue.text: Macmillan's preference George, with wonderment, heard

indicators.note: heard means the words are spoken and caught by ear

parts.note: the name George followed by awe, which is wonderment

explanation.surface: A man named George shows his amazement to be heard.
explanation.walkthrough: Harold Macmillan, British prime minister, said talking is better than war; 'George awe' said quickly sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Macmillan preferred talks and negotiation over fighting, the 'better than war-war' line.

clue.text: Counter from judge upset me, for one

indicators.note: upset in a down entry turns the word upside down

parts.note: me (mi) is an example of a musical note in sol-fa

explanation.surface: A judge's counter-argument that upset the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Me' is the sol-fa syllable, a note; 'upset' reverses NOTE to ETON.
explanation.definitionFit: A token used in games or as a substitute coin is a counter.

clue.text: One ITV acquire to play a typical local?

indicators.note: to play means the letters are worked into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A television channel buying the rights to stage a show about a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The Queen Vic is the pub in the BBC soap EastEnders, and a pub of this name is a common British local.
explanation.definitionFit: Many British pubs are named after the monarch, so it is a typical name for a local pub.

clue.text: Old prior to look for an audience

indicators.note: for an audience means the word is said aloud to listeners

parts.note: an air is a look or appearance

explanation.surface: An elderly prior seeks people to hear him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prior' looks like a monk but is 'before'; 'for an audience' gives ERE from the sound of AIR.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for before, so an old way of saying prior to.

clue.text: Come round on time before Easter

parts.note: re means on, concerning
Lent is the period of fasting before Easter

explanation.surface: Visit promptly before the Easter holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: To give in after resisting is to come round to another view.

clue.text: Guy's initial dread, meeting leading female criminal

indicators.note: initial means the first letter of the name

parts.note: angst is dread or anxiety
ER is the Queen, Elizabeth Regina, the leading woman

explanation.surface: A man's early fear on meeting a woman who leads a gang.
explanation.walkthrough: ER is the Queen, Elizabeth Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of an organised gang is a type of criminal.
